body: cc @whatwg/fieldset

Containing block size calculation (for e.g. percentage height resolution) for legends needs to be specced. I imagine it should contain the logical top border and padding areas (since legends are placed above the padding area, and *are part of* the border), although no browsers do that currently:

http://software.hixie.ch/utilities/js/live-dom-viewer/?saved=6133 (only testing borders, no padding)

Edge/Firefox/Chrome renders the percentage height testcase the same though, so I think we should spec that rather than risk regressing existing web content. Also, I don't consider a rendered legend to be "part of the border" because then its extent should be part of the border-box area and thus the fieldset background should render behind it (fully), a box-shadow should wrap it etc, and that's not what any UAs do as far as I know.

Perhaps the spec would benefit from an example figure that visualizes the rendering? Something like [this table figure](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-tables-3/#example-c06d1eca). In Gecko we implement the `<fieldset>` using two boxes, an outer box that contains the rendered legend as the first child box and an inner anonymous box that contains the boxes of the other `<fieldset>` children. (Similar to how the table wrapper box wraps its caption and an inner table box.) Then it would be easier to discuss where and how the margin/padding/border of the various boxes should be applied and how a "reserved space" for the rendered legend should be calculated.

Yes, all browsers render the same with my test, and I do agree that it's risky to spec it otherwise then. However, since legends are placed at the very top of the fieldset (and thus ignores top border and padding), it's kind of strange that top border and padding are included in the containing block size when resolving percentages.

Anyway, my post about containing block size calculation concerns was written under the assumption that we really let the legend be part of the border area (that's what the current spec changes in this pull request say), but I believe this is something we still need to discuss.

I was quite sold on the "two boxes" approach myself, but then I noticed that WebKit just puts it in the border area (and expands the border area if necessary), which seems simpler, and also easy to reason about. Blink doesn't use two boxes for tables, like the spec says (that implementation detail isn't leaked via any web-exposed API that I'm aware of, though), but what I find tricky with this approach is to determine which properties should be set on the outer box and which to set on the inner one. https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS22/tables.html#model mentions  'position', 'float', 'margin-*', 'top', 'right', 'bottom', and 'left'  as properties to set on the wrapper box. That list is far from complete, though. First of all, it only covers CSS 2 (and even then it seems to forget about things like z-index). How do you determine which property goes where?

EDIT: Looks like the answer to that lies in https://dxr.mozilla.org/mozilla-central/source/layout/style/res/forms.css
Related bug re percentage height. https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=178782

The B result in Firefox seems like a bug to me. I think it should be 150px. I filed [bug 1485646](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1485646).
In that case, I *think* what https://drafts.csswg.org/css2/visudet.html#containing-block-details says should just apply to fieldset, without HTML having to say anything in particular. Right?

I'd like us to settle on a FIELDSET/LEGEND layout model. ```
legend
contents
``` In this example we have a scrollable fieldset. The legend is not expected to scroll along with the fieldset contents, according to Firefox, Safari, and common sense. This does suggest that it makes sense to create an anonymous child for the actual contents of the fieldset. So I'd like to explore that approach a bit further (rather than my former favorite: slap the legend in the border area, expand the border as necessary, paint it as part of border painting - like WebKit). The question then is, which properties should the anonymous child inherit, and which ones should the parent fieldset ignore (if any). And how much magic do we have to apply in addition to that? Intuitively, 'overflow' should go on the anoymous child, so that the legend isn't scrolled along with the rest. Padding probably needs to be ignored on the parent FIELDSET and be applied on the anonymous child, though, so that the scrollport includes the padding. However, percentages need to be resolved on the FIELDSET and NOT on the anonymous child. @MatsPalmgren Does Firefox really get away with no special magic here? Firefox has a nice selector for the anonymous child here: https://dxr.mozilla.org/mozilla-central/source/layout/style/res/forms.css
Why doesn't the WebKit approach work when there is a scrollport? What does WebKit do in that case?

In the normal case it works fine in WebKit, but it just fails to paint the legend completely if the legend establishes a stacking node (position:relative, opacity:0.5, etc.). That changes paint order, and doing it as part of border painting won't do anymore. The legend is a child of what establishes the scrollport (the fieldset), so making it not scroll when it's actually a child is a bit weird, and implementation-wise something new and obviously unsupported. And it'd need to be specced in the layout model somehow, as this is something special.
Hmm yeah that's not acceptable. Would it work to pull it out and make it a (previous?) sibling of the fieldset box?

> This does suggest that it makes sense to create an anonymous child for the actual contents of the fieldset.

That is indeed what Gecko currently does.  Our box tree for your example is:
```
FieldSet(fieldset)
  Block(legend)
      Text "legend"
  HTMLScroll(fieldset) :-moz-fieldset-content
    ScrollbarFrame(scrollbar)
    ScrollbarFrame(scrollbar)
    Box(scrollcorner)
    Block(fieldset) :-moz-scrolled-content
        Block(div)
            Text "contents"
```
The rule for `:-moz-fieldset-content` is here:
https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/source/layout/style/res/forms.css#13-54
and `:-moz-scrolled-content` here:
https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/source/layout/style/res/ua.css#190-234

For comparison, when the `<fieldset>` isn't scrollable the box tree looks like this:
```
FieldSet(fieldset)
  Block(legend)
      Text "legend"
  Block(fieldset) :-moz-fieldset-content
      Block(div)
          Text "contents"
```

> Does Firefox really get away with no special magic here?

Not really. We implement fieldset layout with a specific box type ("frame" in Gecko lingo) and here's the layout code for flowing that:
https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/source/layout/forms/nsFieldSetFrame.cpp#370
and we also have some magic in box construction to create the right box type for the innermost wrapper box based on the outer `display` value. E.g. `<fieldset style="display:grid">...`:
```
FieldSet(fieldset)
  Block(legend)
      Text "legend"
  GridContainer(fieldset) :-moz-fieldset-content
      Block(div)
          Text "contents"
```

> However, percentages need to be resolved on the FIELDSET and NOT on the anonymous child.

Right, that's [a bug](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1485646) we need to fix.

In general though, wrapping the fieldset contents (apart from the rendered legend) seems to work fine.  Complicated stuff like scrolling, grid/flex/column layout etc comes mostly for free with that.

Thanks @MatsPalmgren . Sorry for being unclear, but my test case doesn't demonstrate any bug in Gecko. It works great! Padding is resolved correctly with respect to the containing block, the outer DIV. So, Gecko creates an anonymous HTMLScroll(fieldset) with a Block(fieldset) inside. So, padding is inherited from FieldSet(fieldset) into the HTMLScroll and further into the Block(fieldset), and there it's apparently correctly resolved against the DIV, and at the same time ignored on both the FieldsSet and the HTMLScroll. I see that you have some special code for this. If we say in the spec that we use an anonymous child, we also need to spec this special padding handling somehow.
@MatsPalmgren @mstensho Do we need the `Block(fieldset) :-moz-scrolled-content` part in the spec for the scrollable case? Or is it enough to say that there is a scrollport?
@MatsPalmgren @mstensho please see https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3934/commits/a96084d31456c91cb2a08a738bea022fb06fa736 . I don't know what I'm doing here, help would be much appreciated. :)
In https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1488228 the `align` attribute was discussed. Currently it seems Mats and Morten agree that it should work more like Gecko than like WebKit/Chromium.

Notes from @bzbarsky about what Gecko does

> Fieldset box has two child boxes: legend and content container.
> 
> Legend box is a block formatting context (no matter what display type is 
> used for the legend, pretty much).
> 
> Content container box can be a flex container or a grid container (when 
> the fieldset display is flex/grid respectively) or a block formatting 
> context.  In the latter case it can have columns going on.
> 
> Content container styled via 
> https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/6201a9e0067cf6af118c6a99ae9314b8ceb2c4d5/layout/style/res/forms.css#13-54
> 
> Block-start border does not get painted under legend's border-rect.
> 
> Block-start border is "vertically" (depends on writing mode) centered on 
> legend (both when border width is less than legend's border-box and when 
> it's more, looks like).
> 
> Intrinsic inline sizes, min and preferred, are the max of those sizes 
> for the legend and the content container.
> 
> When our computed block size is not "auto", the "legend space" (which is 
> the extra the legend sticks out past the border) is subtracted from it.

Revamp how fieldset and legend rendering is defined

Properly define the rendering of the fieldset and legend elements.

The layout model used is most similar to Gecko, which uses an anonymous box to hold the fieldset's contents.

Fixes #3955, fixes #3930, fixes #3929, fixes #3928, fixes #3927, fixes #3915, fixes #3913, fixes #3660, fixes #3331, fixes #2756, fixes #4013.
